sections.h2: What is property tax like in Bath County, Kentucky?
sections.html:
Bath County is a rural county of about 279 square miles in the eastern Bluegrass, and its property tax system is run from a handful of courthouse offices in Owingsville. The Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) values land and homes, the sheriff collects the bill, and the county clerk records deeds and handles unpaid bills.

The county was formed in 1811 from Montgomery County and takes its name from mineral springs once thought to have healing properties. Owingsville is the seat and largest city, with Salt Lick and Sharpsburg as the other incorporated cities. Interstate 64 runs through the county, and the Daniel Boone National Forest and Cave Run Lake cover a large share of the land, which limits what can be built and keeps much of the housing stock spread along rural roads.

sections.h2: How many people and homes does Bath County have?
sections.html:
The 2020 Census counted 12,750 residents, and the July 2025 estimate is 13,176, a gain of 3.4 percent. All of the population lives in rural areas, according to the Census count summarized by Wikipedia.

Census QuickFacts for 2020 to 2024 give a picture of the market a seller faces:

  • Owner occupied homes are valued at a median of $129,800, and 74.7 percent of homes are owner occupied.
  • Median gross rent is $659 a month.
  • Median household income is $56,541, and 22.6 percent of residents are in poverty.
  • The mean travel time to work is 30.0 minutes, the longest among the four Kentucky counties in these Census tables, so a longer drive to work is part of daily life here.
  • No building permits were recorded in 2025.

With few new homes being built, older houses make up almost all of what sells in Bath County. Age brings deferred repairs, and a PVA record that has not been updated can overstate or understate what a house is worth.

sections.h2: Which Bath County office does what?
sections.html:
The Bath County government site lists the elected officials and their courthouse contacts. Offices are in Owingsville, and mail goes to separate post office boxes, so address a payment or an appeal to the right one.

  • PVA: assessments, homestead applications and appeal conferences, at (606) 674-6382.
  • Sheriff: tax bills and collection, at (606) 674-2931.
  • County Clerk: deeds, liens, mortgages and, after April 15, delinquent bills, at (606) 674-2613.
  • County Attorney: notices and payment plans on delinquent bills.

The clerk's website carries a delinquent tax page, so you can check whether a parcel appears.

sections.h2: What is the Bath County property tax calendar?
sections.html:
The assessment is set as of January 1 and appeals happen in May, bills go out in the fall, and the collection cycle runs through April 15. The table puts the steps in order using the statutes and the Department of Revenue.

Kentucky property tax calendar as it applies in Bath County
StepTiming
Assessment dateJanuary 1
Tax roll inspection and PVA conferencesFirst Monday in May for two weeks
Filing with county clerkNo later than one workday after inspection closes
Board of assessment appeals sits25 to 35 days after inspection closes, one to five days
Pay with 2 percent discountThrough November 1
Pay face amountNovember 2 to December 31
5 percent penaltyJanuary 1 to 31
10 percent penalty plus sheriff add-onAfter January 31 until April 15

Source: KRS 133.030, KRS 134.015 and the Kentucky Department of Revenue.

If bills are delayed, the state can approve an alternative calendar, giving one month for each stage. A bill for omitted property or an increase after an appeal is due on the day it is prepared.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Bath County assessment?
sections.html:
Ask the Bath County PVA for a conference during the inspection period in May. If you reach an agreement, nothing further is needed. If not, you file at the county clerk's office and state the value you claim.

The local board of assessment appeals has three members and sits in Owingsville, the county seat, under KRS 133.030. The board gets orientation on its first day, reviews recent sales of comparable homes, and can inspect properties in dispute. It may sit for no more than five days after convening unless the Department of Revenue extends the time. You will receive the decision by certified mail.

  • Gather sales of similar homes from the past year, photos of defects, and any appraisal.
  • Ask the PVA to show how the value was reached, since the office keeps records of comparable sales.
  • Bring a repair estimate if the house has a roof, well or septic problem the record does not capture.

You cannot dispute value when the tax bill arrives, because the appeal window has already closed.

sections.h2: Who gets the homestead exemption in Bath County?
sections.html:
Owners who are 65 or older, or totally disabled, may claim it for the home they own and live in. File the application with the Bath County PVA in the year you want the exemption, with proof of age or disability.

KRS 132.810 requires the owner to maintain the property as a personal residence and grants one exemption per residential unit. The dollar amount is indexed to the cost of living and reviewed every two years, so ask the PVA for the current figure. A mobile home or manufactured house can qualify, which matters in a rural county where many owners live in one. Owners who qualify after paying the bill are entitled to a refund of the tax on the exempt amount.

If you sell or the owner dies, the statute requires a report of the transfer to the PVA, and the buyer or heir applies separately.

sections.h2: What happens to unpaid Bath County taxes?
sections.html:
After April 15, unpaid bills transfer from the Bath County Sheriff to the county clerk as certificates of delinquency with a recorded lien. Interest runs at 1 percent monthly, and a clerk fee of 10 percent and a county attorney fee of 20 percent are added, the Department of Revenue says.

County officials must advertise the delinquent parcels and send notices before a summer tax sale, where a third party can buy the certificate and add its own fees. The tax is also the personal debt of the person who owned the property on January 1, and under KRS 134.015 the lien can follow the property for 11 years.

A Bath County owner with a house that needs work and a tax bill that has gone to the clerk can still sell. The payoff is taken from the proceeds at closing, and the clerk quotes the amount for the month. Sellers weighing a listing against a cash sale can compare the net after repairs, back taxes and carrying costs.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Bath County property tax?
faqs.a: Pay the Bath County Sheriff in Owingsville. The county site lists the sheriff's office at (606) 674-2931, and bills are mailed in the fall.

faqs.q: When can I appeal a Bath County assessment?
faqs.a: Only during the tax roll inspection period, which begins the first Monday in May and lasts two weeks. Hold a PVA conference first, then file with the clerk within one workday after it closes.

faqs.q: What is the median home value in Bath County?
faqs.a: The Census Bureau reports a median of $129,800 for owner occupied homes in 2020 to 2024, with 74.7 percent of homes owner occupied.

faqs.q: Does Bath County have a homestead exemption?
faqs.a: Yes. Owners aged 65 or older or totally disabled can apply to the PVA under KRS 132.810. The exemption is for one home you own and live in.

faqs.q: What if my Bath County tax bill goes to the clerk?
faqs.a: The clerk adds interest and fees, and the bill can be sold to a third party at a summer sale. Contact the clerk for a payoff, and the county attorney about a payment plan.
